evals.prompt: Define a rendering model in 2-3 sentences. Name the two axes that distinguish models and give two example named models that land in different cells.
expected_elements: Defines it as the strategy by which a web UI is produced and delivered
Names the two axes: WHEN the work happens (build / request / stream / interaction) and WHERE it executes (server / edge / client)
Notes the named models are cells or paths through that grid (e.g. SSG at build/server, SSR at request/server, CSR at interaction/client)
States the choice determines first-paint, time-to-interactive, server cost, cache behavior, and crawlability

evals.prompt: Why is the rendering-model choice described as per-route rather than per-application?
expected_elements: Different routes have different content profiles (static / dynamic / personalized)
A single model picked for the whole app is wrong for most routes
Each route should land at the grid position matching its content profile and performance constraints
Gives a contrast (e.g. a marketing page wants SSG, a search-results page wants SSR/streaming SSR)

evals.prompt: Compare how SSG, SSR, and CSR differ across first-paint (FCP/LCP), time-to-interactive (TTI), and server cost. Why does no single model dominate?
expected_elements: SSG: best first-paint (CDN-cached HTML), lowest request-time server cost; still pays hydration cost for TTI
SSR: good first-paint (HTML served), highest server cost (render per request), hydration cost for TTI
CSR: worst first-paint (empty shell, client fetch + JS execute) but lowest server cost
Each performance number responds differently to each model, so the right model depends on the route's content profile

evals.prompt: A product-detail page shows a mostly static layout plus a per-user 'recommended for you' block and live inventory. Which model(s) fit and why?
expected_elements: PPR fits: static shell at build time + streamed dynamic holes (recommendations, inventory) at request time
ISR is a reasonable alternative for the catalog portion if updates are periodic
SSR is the fallback if the dynamic portion dominates or catalog changes very frequently
Reasons from the content profile (mostly static with small personalized regions), not from a framework default

evals.prompt: Why might a page that is correctly server-rendered (fast FCP) still feel slow to the user, and what reduces that cost?
expected_elements: Hydration cost: the HTML is produced fast but the page is not interactive until client JS loads, parses, executes
Hydration is visible in TTI and INP and is independent of HTML production speed
Reduction strategies: RSC (server components excluded from the client bundle), islands architecture, progressive hydration, resumability
A large client bundle (e.g. 2MB) hydrates slowly regardless of how the HTML was produced

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the rendering-models skill to decide the folder structure and module layering of the frontend codebase. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Not in scope — codebase organization (folder structure, routing convention, build config) is frontend-architecture
rendering-models owns WHERE and WHEN the UI is produced, an orthogonal decision
A route's architecture and its rendering model are independent decisions
Correctly redirects to frontend-architecture rather than answering out of lane

evals.prompt: A stakeholder frames every rendering decision as 'SSR vs CSR.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: SSR-vs-CSR is not the complete dichotomy; the space is 6-8 named models on a time × place grid
The meaningful comparisons are model-vs-model per route profile (e.g. SSG vs ISR vs SSR for a catalog, streaming SSR vs RSC for a slow dashboard, PPR vs SSR for static + personalization)
Collapsing to a binary makes the real trade-off invisible — a team 'doing SSR' might actually want SSG, RSC, or streaming SSR
The wrong choice is invisible until measured

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a site's rendering-model strategy is implemented correctly?
expected_elements: The model for each route is documented per-route (not per-app) and matches the route's content profile
FCP, LCP, INP are measured in real-user conditions, not lab-only Lighthouse
Hydration cost is acknowledged separately from rendering cost (a fast-SSR page with a large bundle is not actually fast)
SSG/ISR caches invalidate correctly on content updates; edge routes confirm their data access path works at the edge (HTTP-accessible, not direct DB)
